'''Igor Ekhielevich Dzyaloshinskii''', (Игорь Ехиельевич Дзялошинский, surname sometimes transliterated as '''Dzyaloshinsky''', '''Dzyaloshinski''', '''Dzyaloshinskiĭ''', or '''Dzyaloshinkiy''', 1{{nbsp}}February 1931{{snd}}14{{nbsp}}July 2021)<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nauka.tass.ru/nauka/11912339 |title=Умер один из основателей Института теоретической физики РАН Дзялошинский |author= |website= tass.ru|date=15 July 2021 |language=ru}}</ref> was a Russian theoretical physicist, known for his research on "magnetism, [[multiferroics]], [[Conductance quantum|one-dimensional conductors]], [[liquid crystal]]s, [[van der Waals force]]s, and applications of methods of [[quantum field theory]]".<ref name=obitPT>{{cite journal|author=Chernyshev, Alexander|author2=Maradudin, Alexei|author3=Piatevskii, Lev|title=Obituary. Igor Ekhiel'evich Dzyaloshinskii|journal=Physics Today|volume=4|issue=10|page=71|year=2021|doi=10.1063/PT.3.4863|s2cid=244226442|doi-access=free}}</ref> In particular he is known for the [[Antisymmetric exchange|Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Igor Dzyaloshinskii of Physics & Astronomy turns 90 today|date=February 1, 2021|author=Chernyshev, Sasha|website=UCI Physical Sciences Communications|url=https://ps.uci.edu/news/2323}}</ref><ref>Abrikosov ''et al.'': ''Igor' Ekhiel'evich Dzyaloshinskii (on his seventieth birthday)'', Phys. Uspekhi, Vol. 44, 2001, p. 213</ref>

==Biography==
He was born in Moscow to a Jewish family. His father, Yechiel Moiseevich Dzyaloshinskii (1897–1942), a native of [[Kalush, Ukraine]], died in captivity in early 1942.

The first in his family to attend a university,<ref name=obitPT/> Igor E. Dzyaloshinskii graduated in 1953 from the faculty of physics of [[Moscow State University]].<ref name=letopis/>

Dzyaloshinski pursued graduate study at the Institute of Physics of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]], where he received in 1957 his Russian [[Candidate of Sciences]] degree (Ph.D.) with a thesis on weak ferromagnetism under the supervision of [[Lev Landau]].<ref name=letopis>[http://letopis.msu.ru/peoples/4531 Дзялошинский Игорь Ехиельевич, Статья на сайте «Летопись Московского университета» (article from "Chronicle of Moscow State University)]</ref> Weak ferromagnetism is "a small spontaneous magnetic moment in certain classes of antiferromagnetic materials". Its explanation involves [[exchange interaction]]s based upon "concepts of the magnetic symmetry of crystals".<ref>{{cite web|author=Borovik-Romanov, A. S.|title="Weak Ferromagnetism" in ''The Great Soviet Encyclopedia'', 3rd Edition (1970-1979)|url=https://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/Weak+Ferromagnetism}}</ref>

In 1962 Dzyaloshinskii received his Russian [[Doctor of Sciences]] degree ([[habilitation]]). His Russian doctoral thesis dealt with application of quantum field theory methods in statistical physics.<ref name=letopis/> In 1964 he was one of the founding members of the [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Moscow.<ref name=obitPT/> He was until 1972 a professor at the [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]]<ref name=interview>{{cite web|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/5456/1/hrst.mit.edu/hrs/renormalization/Dzyaloshinskii/index.htm|title=Interview with Igor E. Dzyaloshinskii, Irvine, California, 14–13 December 2001|website=Physics of Scale, History of Recent Science & Technology, library.caltech.edu}}</ref> and from 1972 to 1989 at Moscow State University.<ref name=letopis/>

Between 1958 and 1961, with [[Alexei Abrikosov (physicist)|Alexei Abrikosov]] and [[Lev Gor'kov]], he published important works on the application of methods of [[quantum field theory]] in statistical physics (''e.g.'' the theory of superconductivity) and many-particle theory, about which the three also wrote an outstanding textbook Методы квантовой теории поля в статистической физике, which was published in Russian in 1961 and in English translation as ''Quantum field theory methods in statistical physics'' in 1963. Dzaloshinskii did important research with [[Lev Pitaevskii]] in solving "the problem of the van der Waals forces between bodies separated by an absorbing liquid" and with Yury Bychkov and Lev Gor'kov on the "problem of superconducting and charge-density-wave instabilities in 1D conductors".<ref name=obitPT/> Dzyaloshinskii and [[Anatoly Larkin]] in the 1970s published "a solution to the [[Luttinger liquid|Luttinger-liquid]] problem that is central to the theory of 1D Fermi systems and to the bosonization technique."<ref name=obitPT/><ref>{{cite book|doi=10.1142/9789814317344_0014|chapter=''Correlation functions for a one-dimensional Fermi system with long-range interaction (Tomonaga model)'' by I. E. Dzyaloshinskii and A. I. Larkin|title=30 Years of the Landau Institute — Selected Papers|series=World Scientific Series in 20th Century Physics|year=1996|volume=11|pages=95–101|isbn=978-981-02-2253-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Dzyaloshinskii, I.E.|author2=Larkin, A.I.|year=1974|title=Correlation functions for a one-dimensional Fermi system with long-range interaction (Tomonaga model)|journal=Sov. Phys. JETP|volume=38|page=202}}</ref>

In 1991 he immigrated to the United States and soon became a professor at the [[University of California, Irvine]] (UCI), where he eventually retired as professor emeritus.<ref name=obitPT/> In the last years of his career, he did research on violation of time-parity in magneto-optics and the condensed matter physics of [[Fermi liquid theory|Fermi liquid]]s and [[Fermi liquid theory#Non-Fermi liquids|non-Fermi liquids]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Igor E. Dzyaloshinskii|website=UCI Faculty Profile System|url=http://www.faculty.uci.edu/profile.cfm?faculty_id=2312}}</ref>

Dzyaloshinskii applied diagram methods to finite-temperature transport problems. He conjectured the existence of phase transitions without fixed points of the [[renormalization group]]. He was involved in the formulation of the Matsubara formalism ([[Takeo Matsubara]], 1955).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Matsubara, T., Fetter, A. L., Walecka, J. D., Abrikosov, A. A., Gorkov, L. P., & Dzyaloshinski, I. E.|year=1955|title=Quantum theory of many-particle systems: Methods of quantum field theory in statistical physics|journal=Prog. Theor. Phys.|volume=14|page=351|doi=10.1143/PTP.14.351|s2cid=119767087 }}</ref>

Dzyaloshinskii  was awarded in 1972 the Lomonosov Prize, in 1975 the [[Order of the Badge of Honour]], in 1981 the [[Order of the Red Banner of Labour]], in 1984 the [[USSR State Prize]], and in 1989 the [[Landau Prize]]. He was elected in 1974 a corresponding member of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences|Soviet Academy of Sciences]], in 1991 an honorary foreign member of the [[American Academy of Arts & Sciences]], in 1996 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], and in 2002 a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.physics.uci.edu/awards#alphabetical |title=Igor Dzyaloshinskii |website=Faculty Honors & Awards (alphabetical list), Dept. of Physics and Astronomy, UCI}}</ref>

He married in 1960.<ref name=interview/> Upon his death, he was survived by his widow, their daughter, three grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web|title=Igor Dzyaloshinkii, a towering figure in theoretical physics, has passed away|date=July 16, 2021|author=Chernyshev, Sasha|website=UCI Physical Sciences Communications|url=https://ps.uci.edu/news/2453}}</ref>
